draft.title: Antidifferentiation
card: Antidifferentiation reverses differentiation. If f′(x) = 2x, then f(x) could be x², because the derivative of x² is 2x.
Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power. The antiderivative of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Do each term of a sum separately.
The constant c is needed because a constant has derivative 0. So x², x² + 5 and x² − 3 all have derivative 2x. They form a family of curves with the same gradient at each x value.
A known point picks out one curve. Example: f′(x) = 6x² and f(1) = 5. Then f(x) = 2x³ + c. Put in x = 1: 2 + c = 5, so c = 3 and f(x) = 2x³ + 3.
draft.remember: Antidifferentiate to get xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, then use a known point to find c.

a.q: Which function has derivative f′(x) = 4x³ and passes through (1, 7)?
a.why: The antiderivative of 4x³ is x⁴ + c. Putting in x = 1 gives 1 + c = 7, so c = 6. The option x⁴ + 7 has the right shape, but it gives 8 at x = 1, not 7, as it uses the y value as c.
a.clue: Find x⁴ + c first, then put in the point.

b.q: A curve has gradient 3x² − 4x at every point and passes through (2, 1). What is its equation?
b.why: The antiderivative is y = x³ − 2x² + c. At x = 2: 8 − 8 + c = 1, so c = 1. The option with no constant would give y = 0 at x = 2, not 1. The option with −4x² divides by the new power wrongly: it leaves out the division by 2.
b.clue: Divide each term by its new power, then use (2, 1) to find c.

final.title: Antidifferentiation
card: Antidifferentiation reverses differentiation. If \(f'(x) = 2x\), then \(f(x)\) could be \(x^{2}\), because the derivative of \(x^{2}\) is \(2x\).
Add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power. The antiderivative of \(x^{n}\) is \(\frac{x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + c\), for \(n \ne -1\). Do each term of a sum separately.

The constant \(c\) is needed because a constant has derivative 0. So \(x^{2}\), \(x^{2} + 5\) and \(x^{2} - 3\) all have derivative \(2x\). They form a family of curves with the same gradient at each value of \(x\).
A known point picks out one curve. Example: \(f'(x) = 6x^{2}\) and \(f(1) = 5\). Then \(f(x) = 2x^{3} + c\). Put in \(x = 1\): \(2 + c = 5\), so \(c = 3\) and \(f(x) = 2x^{3} + 3\).
final.remember: Antidifferentiate to get \(\frac{x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + c\), then use a known point to find \(c\).

a.q: Which function has derivative \(f'(x) = 4x^{3}\) and passes through \((1, 7)\)?
a.why: The antiderivative of \(4x^{3}\) is \(x^{4} + c\). Putting in \(x = 1\) gives \(1 + c = 7\), so \(c = 6\). The option \(x^{4} + 7\) has the right shape, but it gives 8 at \(x = 1\), not 7, as it uses the y-value as \(c\).
a.clue: Find \(x^{4} + c\) first, then put in the point.

b.q: A curve has gradient \(3x^{2} - 4x\) at every point and passes through \((2, 1)\). What is its equation?
b.why: The antiderivative is \(y = x^{3} - 2x^{2} + c\). At \(x = 2\): \(8 - 8 + c = 1\), so \(c = 1\). The option with no constant would give \(y = 0\) at \(x = 2\), not 1. The option with \(-4x^{2}\) divides by the new power wrongly: it leaves out the division by 2.
b.clue: Divide each term by its new power, then use \((2, 1)\) to find \(c\).
